name: Pricing Illiquid Assets
title: Pricing Illiquid Assets
answer: Pricing illiquid assets covers the valuation of holdings that do not trade on a public market, such as private equity, private credit, real estate, infrastructure, and stakes in private companies. In portfolio construction the topic matters because reported values can be stale, smoothed, or model dependent, which affects risk estimates, allocation drift, and performance reporting. The work sits between accounting fair value, appraisal practice, and quantitative portfolio analysis. It also covers the liquidity premium, the cost of exiting a position, and the difference between a mark for reporting and a price for trading.

sections.body: Pricing illiquid assets covers the valuation of holdings that do not trade on a public market, such as private equity, private credit, real estate, infrastructure, and stakes in private companies. In portfolio construction the topic matters because reported values can be stale, smoothed, or model dependent, which affects risk estimates, allocation drift, and performance reporting. The work sits between accounting fair value, appraisal practice, and quantitative portfolio analysis. It also covers the liquidity premium, the cost of exiting a position, and the difference between a mark for reporting and a price for trading.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on data pipelines that combine fund administrator reports, general partner statements, capital account statements, cash flow histories, and deal documents. Public market proxies, such as the 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices tracked on this site, can inform beta and discount rate assumptions when direct comparables are thin. Transaction evidence, including the 355 merger and acquisition filings tracked here, supports precedent transaction analysis and calibration of exit assumptions. Valuation models, scenario engines, and document stores sit on cloud or on-premise infrastructure, with version control and audit logs for every input and assumption.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts typically start with a discounted cash flow model, then triangulate against comparable companies, precedent transactions, and, where relevant, option pricing or Monte Carlo simulation. Because private marks can be smoothed, practitioners often unsmooth reported returns, adjust for stale pricing, and test sensitivity to discount rates, exit multiples, and timing. Machine learning appears in comparable selection, document extraction, and anomaly detection, but the final valuation usually passes through a committee that documents judgment. The output feeds portfolio construction through expected returns, covariance estimates, liquidity budgets, and stress tests rather than a single point estimate.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Governance covers fair value standards, valuation policies, independent review, audit trails, and disclosure to limited partners and regulators. Provenance matters because every input, from a broker quote to a management projection, needs a source, a date, and a rationale, and conflicts of interest must be managed when the same firm manages the asset and values it. Risks include stale or smoothed marks, model error, selection bias in comparables, and litigation over reported performance. This site's 219 compliance and regulation pages provide reference material on the rules and expectations that shape these controls, though the specific obligations depend on jurisdiction and fund terms.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more frequent valuation, greater use of real-time data, and tighter integration between valuation and portfolio risk systems. Private market secondaries, tokenized fund interests, and daily net asset value reporting are pushing valuation cycles shorter, while regulators and investors ask for more transparency into assumptions. AI-assisted comparable analysis and document review are likely to reduce manual effort, but they also raise questions about model validation and data lineage. The practical result for portfolio construction is a continuing shift from periodic marks toward a continuous, auditable view of liquidity and value.
